overview: Quantitative reasoning tests your number skills: addition, times tables, brackets and division, all worked under time pressure. In IQ tests it appears as short numerical problems where both speed and accuracy count. Quick, reliable mental arithmetic frees your attention for the harder reasoning that follows.

strategy.b: Rapid recall of sums and times tables saves time on every question. Drill the facts until you can answer them without counting on your fingers. The time you save adds up across a whole test.

Split large numbers into easier pieces, such as 47 + 38 becoming 47 + 30 + 8. You can also round one number to a friendly value, then correct the answer afterwards. Choose whichever split keeps the working simplest.

Work out brackets first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. Writing each step on paper prevents slips when a question has several parts. Check the order before you start calculating.

Work out a rough answer first so you can rule out options that are clearly wrong. Compare your exact answer with the estimate to catch arithmetic slips. Estimating also saves time when two options look close.

fig.title: Order of working
fig.note: Work left to right within each group.

drills.name: Quick sums
drills.how: Split one number into tens and units, then add each part to the other number in turn. Start with the larger number, which keeps the working short.
drills.tip: Round to the nearest ten, then adjust the answer by the amount you rounded.
drills.mistake: Forgetting to carry a ten when adding columns, which makes the answer off by ten or a hundred. Write the carried digit above the next column before you add it.

ex.why: Add 40 to 48 to get 88, then take away 3 to get 85.

drills.name: Times tables
drills.how: Learn the facts in small groups, such as the 6s and 7s, then practise them in random order. Use patterns, such as the digits of any 9 times answer adding to 9, to check quickly.
drills.tip: Say each fact aloud as you write it to strengthen recall.
drills.mistake: Practising in strict order, so you remember the sequence rather than each answer on its own. Mix the facts up so every one is recalled independently.

ex.why: Start from 8 x 8 = 64, then take away one group of 8 to get 56.

drills.name: Multiply and add
drills.how: Work out the multiplication first, then add the result to the other number. Write the product down on its own before you add it.
drills.tip: Multiply before you add, even when the addition comes first in the question.
drills.mistake: Adding first because the question reads left to right, which gives the wrong answer. Multiply first, then add, following the order of operations.

ex.why: Multiply first: 4 x 5 = 20, then add 6 to get 26.

drills.name: Brackets
drills.how: Work out everything inside the brackets first, then use that result in the rest of the calculation. With two sets of brackets, finish the left one before starting the right one.
drills.tip: Circle the bracket on paper so you remember to finish it before the next step.
drills.mistake: Multiplying only the first term inside the brackets, such as turning 3 x (4 + 2) into 12 + 2. Finish the whole bracket first, then multiply the result.

drills.name: Division drills
drills.how: Check each division by multiplying back, such as asking which number times 12 gives 156. Break a large division into smaller steps by taking out the easy parts first.
drills.tip: Learn division facts from the times tables you already know, since they run in reverse.
drills.mistake: Dividing by the wrong number in a two-step question, such as halving when you should divide by three. Write each step on its own line so you can see which number you are using.

levels: Level 1: Sums and facts within 20 using single-digit numbers, with about 30 seconds per question.
Level 2: Two-digit sums and times tables up to 10 x 10, with about 25 seconds per question.
Level 3: Multiply-and-add and bracket questions using small numbers, with about 20 seconds per question.
Level 4: Times tables up to 12 x 12 and two-digit by one-digit multiplication, with about 18 seconds per question.
Level 5: Division and multi-step brackets using three-digit numbers, with about 15 seconds per question.
Level 6: Mixed multi-step problems with larger numbers and decimals, with about 12 seconds per question.
routine: Day 1: Do 20 quick sums, splitting each number into tens and units in your head.
Day 2: Drill the 6, 7 and 8 times tables in random order until each fact takes under two seconds.
Day 3: Work 10 multiply-and-add questions, writing the multiplication step before you add.
Day 4: Solve 10 bracket questions, finishing each bracket before any other step.
Day 5: Do 15 division questions, checking every answer by multiplying back.
